Galactic Lettering as a Reading Environment
        Hand drawing, character encodings, and procedural transformation
                                in Flyxion’s font collection

                                     Flyxion
                                   Independent Researcher

                                October 2026


                                     Abstract
     The font collection in the standardgalactic/fonts repository contains hand-drawn faces
       for Standard Galactic and several related scripts, together with a procedural laboratory
      that turns those faces into thousands of transformed variants. This essay inventories the
       faces, separates what can be measured from the files from what rests on the maker’s ac-
      count, and argues that the collection is best read through one distinction: the intensity of
      a process does not determine the state it leaves behind. A reader’s familiarity with a script
      accumulates along a path of exposure, and a degraded font is the product of either an inde-
      pendent sweep or a cumulative sequence. Treating both as paths, and keeping geometric,
       recognition, and provenance measures apart, yields a set of reader-side experiments that
      the repository is unusually well placed to support.

1  Introduction

Standard Galactic is a substitution alphabet that originated in the Commander Keen games of
id Software and has since gathered a community of users and a block of positions in the Under-
ConScript Unicode Registry [1, 2]. Flyxion’s Galactic fonts have become ordinary instruments
of reading in that community’s sense of the word. SGA Regular has served as a system font
on two computers, and Cursive Galactic is used on a newer machine and for subtitles in VLC.
These uses place the designs in conditions quite different from those of an alphabet chart or
a decorative specimen. A system interface demands repeated recognition of familiar labels,
filenames, numbers, and punctuation, and subtitles demand that recognition take place while
speech, images, and narrative continue. The fonts therefore deserve analysis as parts of a
working reading environment. Their unusual appearance is only the beginning of the subject.
What the files supply, and what can be checked in them, are the conditions under which that
appearance can become familiar.
   The collection supports a more specific claim, and the essay is organized around it.  Fa-
miliarity with a script is cumulative. A reader who has met a letterform ten thousand times
in menus and subtitles occupies a position reached by a particular path of exposure, and two
readers at the same nominal level of practice need not have followed the same path. The

                                         1

procedural tools in the repository make the same distinction available on the side of the stimu-
lus. Its sequence code separates an independent sweep, in which every state is generated from
the original source with its own parameter value, from a cumulative sequence, in which each
state is generated from its predecessor. Its order-effect experiments ask whether applying one
operation and then another gives the same outline as the reverse. In each case the intensity
parameter fails to determine the resulting state, because history enters. The argument of the
essay is that a font state, like a reader state, is a point on a path, and that the repository’s
habit of keeping geometric measurements, recognition scores, and provenance records apart is
the right response to that fact.
   The essay examines the font files in the repository, with particular attention to SGA Reg-
ular and Cursive Galactic, and draws on Flyxion’s account of making glyphs manually with
a Sharpie, using Calligraphr online, and assembling or editing fonts with FontForge. That
account supplies production history which the binaries alone cannot recover.  The analy-
sis distinguishes direct measurements, observations from rendered specimens, documentary
statements in the repository, and interpretations of what these practices make possible.  It
does not presume that every included glyph was drawn by Flyxion or that an inherited
metadata field supplies the complete history of a modified face.  The repository’s own  li-
censing notes take the same position:  they list the provenance of SGA Regular and Cur-
sive Galactic, among others, as not yet recorded  [5].  The snapshot examined  is commit
0d57718b6b69058886de31fe788cbdbe821e77a9.

2  The inventory

The inventory immediately complicates the idea that these are simply fonts for a twenty-six-
letter substitution alphabet. SGA Regular contains 14,208 glyphs and 14,205 mappings in its
preferred Unicode character map. Cursive Galactic contains 1,134 glyphs and 1,132 mappings.
These figures count different things. A glyph is an entry in the font’s repertoire of visual forms,
while a character mapping associates a code point with such an entry. Several characters can
share a glyph, and a glyph can exist without a direct Unicode mapping. Neither number is
equivalent to a count of independently invented signs. The difference matters throughout this
collection, whose faces range from compact handwritten alphabets to extensive multilingual
compilations.
   The principal inventory measured directly from the files is given in Table 1. Private-use
counts describe mapped positions, including any positions containing placeholders, rather than
certified usable characters.
   The table describes the files rather than ranking them. Cheiro can possess fewer glyphs
than mapped characters because several quotation-mark characters point to shared glyphs. A
compact face can accomplish its intended purpose with dozens of forms, whereas a much larger
face can still leave practical gaps. The repository also includes four Amiri faces, whose glyph
counts range from 6,472 to 6,624 and whose preferred Unicode maps cover between 1,548
and 1,699 characters.  Those are explicitly identified as third-party fonts in the repository
documentation.  Their presence is useful comparatively:  substantial inventories can result


                                        2

Font file                        Glyphs  Unicode mappings   Private-use mappings
       Sga-Regular.ttf                    14,208              14,205                  2,307
       CursiveGalactic-Regular.ttf          1,134               1,132                  244
      NovaMonoStandardGalactic.ttf      6,024               6,021                  2,304
       Systada-Regular.ttf                  669                667                  380
       Systada.ttf                         669                667                  380
        dactyl.ttf                           669                667                  380
       Logico_philosophicus-Regular.ttf      283                287                    0
       shapeform.ttf                        81                 78                    0
       Cheiro-Regular.ttf                    66                 70                    0
       Clypto-Regular.ttf                    66                 70                    0
       Lingojam_cipher-Regular.ttf          35                 33                    0

Table 1: Glyph and character-map counts measured from the font files at the examined snap-
shot.

from different design requirements, and the relation between mapped characters and available
glyphs varies sharply between fonts.
  SGA Regular’s extent is chiefly an extent of coexistence. In rendered samples, Latin letters
become Galactic forms, accented Latin letters can become Galactic forms with distinguishing
marks, and many other writing systems retain their conventional appearance. Greek remains
recognizable Greek, Cyrillic remains Cyrillic, and sampled Arabic characters retain Arabic
forms. Mathematical symbols, Braille, arrows, and other signs occupy further parts of the
inventory. The file therefore combines a particular reading transformation with a broad sup-
porting repertoire. This is especially relevant to its use in a desktop environment, where a font
encounters more than continuous English prose. The practical surface includes punctuation,
mathematical expressions, unexpected symbols, and occasional text in other scripts.
   Nevertheless, a character map is not a guarantee of complete language support. A font
can contain Arabic character outlines without supplying all the shaping machinery necessary
for polished Arabic typography. SGA Regular has a GDEF table but neither a GSUB nor
a GPOS table, the OpenType tables commonly used for contextual glyph substitutions and
positioning. This does not make every rendering of complex text impossible, since application
behavior and other mechanisms matter, but it limits the conclusions that can be drawn from
coverage figures. The same caution applies to combining marks, rare letters, and script-specific
conventions. It is more accurate to say that the file carries many kinds of characters than to
claim that it fully supports every language whose characters appear in its map.
   The absence of a shaping layer has a further consequence for the later sections.  The
inspected generators implement degradation primarily through changes to outline geometry.
The absence of GSUB and GPOS does not require this approach: character remapping, metric
changes, raster processing, and application behavior provide other ways to alter rendered text.
Of SGA Regular’s 14,208 glyph entries, 14,175 contain outlines and 33 are empty, and the
outlines together contain 638,671 points, roughly forty-five per glyph on average. Moreover,
11,710 entries have advance widths of either 512 or 1,024 units within a 1,000-unit em, so the
full-width cells slightly exceed the em itself. This concentration is consistent with material


                                         3

organized around half-width and full-width cells. Together with the sharp stylistic differences
between character groups, it suggests a history of compilation and modification: the principal
Galactic forms have rounded, somewhat irregular strokes, whereas numerous other characters
have conspicuously pixel-like outlines. The evidence does not identify the exact source font for
every group. Resemblance to a known broad-coverage font is a lead for further comparison,
rather than proof of descent.
   The table-level statistics sharpen several of these points. The 14,208 glyphs exceed the
14,205 mapped code points by exactly three, and the three unmapped glyphs are .notdef,
.null, and nonmarkingreturn, the housekeeping entries of an ordinary TrueType font. Every
other glyph entry is therefore reached by exactly one code point in the preferred character
map. Unlike Cheiro, the file does not map multiple characters to the same glyph entry in that
map.  Distinct entries can nevertheless contain identical outline data, as the earlier outline
inspection confirmed, so the count does not establish an equal number of visually distinct
designs. The mapped code points divide into 13,821 in the Basic Multilingual Plane and 384
in Plane 1. By Unicode general category the largest groups are other letters (3,630), private
use (2,307), other symbols (1,726), lowercase letters (1,223), and uppercase letters (1,076),
followed by 969 code points that the Unicode data used for the tally does not assign. That
last group should be read with care, since it may reflect characters added to Unicode after the
data was compiled or positions filled with placeholders, and the category alone does not decide
between them. The 816 nonspacing and 209 spacing combining marks are consistent with the
zero-advance overlay mechanism described below for Cistercian numerals, given that no GPOS
table exists to position marks, but this has been checked only for the sampled numerals. All
thirty-two positions from U+EB40 to U+EB5F are mapped even though the registry proposal
assigns twenty-nine, and rendered specimens confirm that the three unused positions display
hexadecimal placeholders. The GDEF table occupies thirty bytes; its contribution must be
determined from its contents rather than its size, since glyph classifications can inform layout
even though GDEF does not itself specify substitutions or positioning adjustments, and the
glyph outlines account for about 1.77 million of the file’s roughly 2.03 million bytes, close to
87 percent.

3  From marker to character address

Flyxion’s account of using a Sharpie gives the central Galactic forms an intelligible material
origin. A felt-tip marker produces width through the contact between a relatively broad nib and
paper, and curved turns, terminal shapes, and small differences in pressure or angle can enter
the resulting silhouette. Digitization preserves selected features of that trace while removing
its paper, scale, and immediate circumstances. The font can then repeat a hand-drawn sign
thousands of times.  Its individuality survives as a reproducible outline. What was once an
event of writing becomes a resource for subsequent writing by anyone using the file.
    It would be excessive to identify the tool solely from the outlines, since similar effects can
be drawn digitally or produced through transformation. Here the material account comes from
the maker, while the specimens show features consistent with it. SGA Regular’s strokes have


                                         4

rounded ends and local irregularities that distinguish them from a strict grid construction.
Several metadata records explicitly identify Calligraphr as the creation tool. SGA Regular’s
unique identifier contains the date string 19 December 2020, Cursive Galactic’s contains 18
May 2024, and Cheiro and Clypto both contain 3 January 2025. These are traces of export or
naming history. Later editing and merging can retain them, so they should not be mistaken
for exhaustive dates of authorship or final revision.
   The movement from marker to Calligraphr and FontForge is consequently more than a
change of medium. It separates outline production from character assignment and deployment.
The drawing supplies a form, a character map determines when that form appears, and spacing
and other metrics determine how it behaves beside neighboring forms. A convincing isolated
glyph can still fail in a line if its spacing is inappropriate, and an accomplished alphabet can
still be inconvenient if the expected punctuation or whitespace is missing. Much of the labor of
making a usable font occurs in these less spectacular relations. A person manually assembling
a font is organizing the conditions under which drawn marks can function repeatedly as text.
  SGA Regular’s two Galactic repertoires make this especially clear.  Its ordinary Latin
A–Z positions render Galactic forms, while the private-use range U+EB40–U+EB59 contains
another rendering of the Galactic letters. The sampled private-use forms are angular and pixel-
like, unlike the rounded Latin-position forms. The file thus distinguishes, in its construction,
between changing how ordinary Latin-coded text looks and displaying separately encoded
Galactic characters. A user can encounter similar alphabetic content through two different
arrangements of character identity and glyph selection.
   The private-use arrangement follows the Under-ConScript Unicode Registry proposal, which
allocates U+EB40–U+EB5F to Standard Galactic. It assigns twenty-six letters, two quotation
marks, and a full stop, leaving three positions unused. The registry coordinates private agree-
ments about character positions, and it does not confer official Unicode assignments.  Its
practical value is nevertheless substantial. Two independently produced fonts can agree that
the same private-use code point means a Galactic letter, allowing text to retain its intended
script identity when moved between those fonts. The convention provides a shared address
system for a community’s writing practices [1, 2].
   Latin-position substitution serves a different practical aim. An existing English subtitle file
can remain unchanged while its appearance becomes Galactic. Search, copying, and other text
operations generally continue to encounter the original Latin characters, subject to the behavior
of the application and document format.  Dedicated private-use Galactic text changes the
underlying character sequence and therefore requires appropriate conversion or input methods
as well as a compatible font.  These approaches have different conveniences.  The former
integrates easily with an existing computer interface, and the latter makes the script distinction
explicit in the stored text. A font that accommodates both can participate in both practices
without forcing every use into one model.





                                        5

4  Registry material and composition

The registry-aligned material extends beyond Standard Galactic. SGA Regular has mappings
throughout the ranges allocated to Tengwar, Cirth, Verdurian, Visible Speech, D’ni, Aurebesh,
Orokin, and Deini, and selected rendered samples show recognizable forms from those systems.
These observations support the claim that the file contains a collection of constructed and
specialized scripts. They do not certify every character of each range. Some blocks contain
assigned positions, unused positions, and placeholders together. A full conformance study
would compare each assigned character with its chart and test its behavior in appropriate text
sequences. The present analysis establishes a substantial pattern without turning sampled
inspection into an exhaustive audit [2, 3].
   Cistercian numerals offer a particularly revealing example because the convention governs
composition as well as individual appearance. The registry proposal assigns spacing units digits
and combining tens, hundreds, and thousands digits within U+EBA0–U+EBDF. In both SGA
Regular and Cursive Galactic, the sampled units digit advances the cursor, while the sampled
higher-place digits have zero advance and outlines extending back into the preceding character’s
area.  This is consistent with building a compound numeral by overlaying its components.
It is a small typographic mechanism: the stored sequence has several characters, but their
spatial arrangement can yield one assembled sign. Exhaustive testing of all combinations and
applications remains outside the present inspection [4].
   This example also explains why placeholders must be interpreted locally. The Cistercian
proposal explicitly leaves positions such as U+EBAA–U+EBAF unused. Boxes bearing those
hexadecimal addresses do not demonstrate a failure to draw the digits, because those positions
do not designate digits in the first place. A placeholder at an assigned position would be a dif-
ferent matter. Broad fonts often preserve these diagnostic forms so that missing or undefined
material remains visible. Their presence contributes to the raw glyph count without contribut-
ing the same kind of writing capacity as a usable character. The inventory is consequently
both a collection of signs and a record of its own boundaries.

5  Cursive Galactic and reading in use

Cursive Galactic reorganizes this environment around a more continuous visual gesture. In the
rendered specimens, its main letters lean, bend, and extend in ways that make their strokes
feel more directional than those of SGA Regular. The word “cursive” should be understood
carefully here. The font contains neither GSUB nor GPOS tables, and the inspected lettering
does not depend on an OpenType system of contextual joins. Its cursiveness is visible chiefly
in the individual forms and their arrangement, rather than demonstrated through a machinery
of neighboring-letter substitutions. The distinction does not diminish the style. A font can
evoke writing in motion without connecting every letter to the next.
   The contrast is most evident at the scale of a line. SGA Regular’s mixture of dots, short
bars, and discrete strokes gives sampled words a segmented texture, while Cursive Galactic
draws more attention to the direction and extension of strokes.  Whether one is easier to
read cannot be decided from those descriptions alone, because size, spacing, display resolution,

                                         6

familiarity, and the particular reader all matter.  Flyxion’s preference for reading subtitles
in the cursive face is evidence about an established personal practice.  It is not a controlled
comparison of population reading speeds.  Its importance is that a design which may look
difficult to an unfamiliar observer has become an effective reading surface for its user.
   Subtitles make that practice especially instructive. Their disappearance imposes a tempo-
ral constraint, since the viewer cannot assume that a line will remain available indefinitely.
Repeated use supplies opportunities to recognize common words and recurring patterns under
that constraint.  It is reasonable to interpret sustained comfortable viewing as evidence of
practical familiarity, while leaving open how that familiarity is implemented psychologically.
No particular neural mechanism need be posited, and no claim is needed that every letter is
processed in a particular sequence. The observable fact is sufficient: an alternative graphic
vocabulary has become compatible with following an ordinary film.
   Using a system font expands that familiarity across tasks. Menus, error messages, filenames,
and settings each furnish recurring encounters with the same repertoire. Their wording often
has strong contextual support, but they also differ in length, importance, and frequency. To-
gether they create a distributed practice environment without requiring a separate lesson. This
gives the fonts an unusual relation to learning. They occupy activities that already matter to
the reader, allowing familiarity to develop through use. The interface becomes both the object
of attention and, intermittently, the background against which other attention takes place. It
is also a clear case of a cumulative path: what the reader can do now depends on the order
and spacing of encounters that cannot be recovered from the present level of skill.

6  The smaller faces and layered authorship

The smaller faces help distinguish this environment from mere inventory size.  Cheiro’s 66
glyphs produce recognizable Latin handwriting with a flowing, rounded character in the ren-
dered sample.  Clypto, also with 66 glyphs, gives the same Latin sentence a more angular
and economical texture. Both support letters and a selection of punctuation, while ordinary
decimal digits are absent from their preferred Unicode maps. A renderer using these files alone
can therefore show missing-character boxes for a numerical specimen, whereas a browser or
desktop with fallback may conceal that limitation by supplying digits from another face. Ap-
parent completeness in an application can be a property of the font environment rather than
of one file.
   Cheiro and Clypto are useful comparisons because they preserve recognizable Latin reading
while varying the drawn vocabulary. Their identity is located substantially in gesture, propor-
tions, and the differentiation of familiar characters. SGA Regular and Cursive Galactic modify
the familiar graphic vocabulary much more decisively, even when the underlying characters
remain Latin. The collection therefore explores several degrees of departure from conventional
typography. This observation concerns what the files do, rather than an assumption that every
face was conceived as part of one systematic research program from the outset.
   Logico_philosophicus supplies a further case.  Its Latin-position specimen renders as an
arrangement of mathematical-looking and logical-looking signs, rather than recognizable Latin


                                        7

handwriting or the usual Galactic forms. Its 283 glyphs support 287 mapped characters. The
effect invites a comparison between reading prose and inspecting formal notation, but the
name and visual vocabulary do not establish a new logical language. Without an additional
grammar and interpretation, substitution changes the appearance of the sentence rather than
its inferential content. Its interest lies partly in that displacement: prose can acquire the visual
atmosphere of formal argument while continuing to be ordinary prose at the character level.
   The Lingojam cipher font demonstrates why a standard pangram is not always an appropri-
ate test. Its 35 glyphs and 33 mappings do not include the ordinary Latin alphabet. Instead,
the map contains selected Canadian syllabic characters, mathematical signs, a katakana char-
acter, and other Unicode symbols. An ordinary English sentence therefore produces missing
characters when rendered in this font alone. That result should not be described as a failed al-
phabet without considering its intended input. The file appears designed to render an already
converted symbol sequence. This is a third arrangement alongside Latin-position substitution
and dedicated private-use encoding: existing Unicode characters serve as the carriers of a visual
cipher.
   Such reuse can be convenient because those characters can already be copied and exchanged
through Unicode text systems.  It also introduces a distinction between their conventional
identities and their intended use in the cipher. A mathematical sign employed as a substitute
letter remains that mathematical character to software which does not know the convention.
The same visible result can therefore conceal quite different underlying structures. Studying
these fonts requires attention to what was typed, what was stored, and what the font actually
drew. A screenshot alone cannot reliably answer all three questions.
   Shapeform pushes the comparison toward compact silhouettes. Its 81 glyphs and 78 map-
pings produce dense, irregular black forms in the inspected Latin-letter sample. Its preferred
map does not include ordinary space or decimal digits, which again makes a conventional
sentence specimen partly a test of unsuitable input.  Its internal family name remains “Un-
titled1,” while a copyright field names Mechachleopteryx and the unique identifier records a
FontForge date string in December 2023. These traces show why filenames, internal names,
and actual visual behavior should all be examined. They need not have been brought into
complete alignment during a manually evolving project.
   Systada and Dactyl reveal another kind of continuity. Systada-Regular, Systada, and Dactyl
each contain 669 glyphs, 667 mappings, and 380 private-use mappings. Their specimens share a
Galactic character, while details such as the treatment of numerals differ. Equal counts do not
prove that the files are identical or establish their exact genealogy. Their metadata provides
further evidence: the Systada files and Dactyl preserve an attribution to Andrew O’Rourke,
with acknowledgments to Fixedsys Excelsior and galax.xyz, while Dactyl has its own internal
naming and a later FontForge identifier. The repository’s licensing notes separately describe
Systada as a mixture of hand-drawn material and glyphs from another typeface whose source
is not yet identified [5]. The repository’s FONTLOG.txt consists of a single line, “Terminal
Friendly Standard Galactic Font,” and does not name a file. On Flyxion’s account it describes
Systada, which gives that family a purpose the other faces lack:  it was made to be read in
a terminal. This is consistent with the Fixedsys Excelsior acknowledgment in the metadata,
since that typeface is a fixed-width system face, but the link between the log line and the font

                                        8

rests on the maker’s statement and not on anything in the file. These are traces of layered
construction, not reasons to assign all the drawing to any one source.
   NovaMonoStandardGalactic is particularly instructive because its filename could lead an
analyst astray. An ordinary Latin pangram renders as recognizable Latin text in the inspected
file.  Its internal family name is “NovaMono for Powerline,” and its metadata records the
NovaMono attribution. It also contains 2,304 private-use mappings. The responsible conclusion
is that this file’s Galactic role cannot be inferred simply from its filename or from assuming
that it performs the same Latin substitution as SGA Regular. The repository’s notes identify
it as a Modified Version of NovaMono under the SIL Open Font License, and they draw the
consequence that follows from the licence: a Modified Version may not keep the Reserved
Font Name, so the family name inside the font as well as the filename should change [5]. The
metadata observation and the legal rule therefore point at the same field. Further glyph-level
comparison would be needed to delimit all of the file’s modifications.
   These histories make authorship a layered matter. A font may include original drawings,
borrowed supporting characters, altered outlines, retained metadata, and newly introduced
mappings. Manual labor can be concentrated in selecting and arranging those relations as
well as in drawing every contour.  Flyxion’s recollection of working through several tools is
compatible with this layered structure. The files do not preserve the whole sequence of decisions,
but neither does the absence of a written design history imply that those decisions were absent.
The licensing notes add a rule for derived material: a font generated from an OFL source
inherits that licence, and one generated from a public-domain source inherits that status.
Provenance in this collection is therefore recorded most completely for the transformations
and least completely for the sources, an asymmetry that matters for any claim about what the
experiments transform.

7  Procedural transformation

The newer repository extends that craft into procedural transformation. At the inspected
snapshot, its complete recursive tree lists 2,418 TTF or OTF paths, including 15 root-level
font files and 2,184 font paths under experiments/. These are file counts, not counts of unique
designs or independent inventions. Additional groups hold earlier experimental versions, styled
variants, debugging outputs, and alterations. The scale is nevertheless meaningful because
it shows how a small set of source faces can become material for a large space of controlled
variations. The handwritten outline becomes a starting condition for later geometric processes.
   The inspected generator implements operations including jitter, shear, quantization, waves,
rotation, contour displacement, and several nonlinear deformation fields. Some affect individual
points, while others move larger parts of a contour coherently or impose spatial divisions. These
differences matter aesthetically and experimentally. Independent noise can roughen a stroke
without preserving the relation between its parts, whereas coherent movement can retain a
recognizable local structure while relocating it. Quantization subjects coordinates to a grid,
producing a different kind of simplification from simple scaling. The experiment names offer
evocative readings of these operations, but their mathematical implementation determines


                                        9

what they actually change.
   The code also distinguishes an independent parameter sweep from a cumulative sequence. In
an independent sweep, each output is generated from the original source with its own parameter
value. In a cumulative sequence, each state is generated from its predecessor. The difference
changes what a progression means. A sequence of increasingly strong deformations need not
contain any accumulated history  if every frame starts again from the source.  Conversely,
cumulative modification can retain earlier disturbances and alter the conditions under which
later ones act. The repository records which kind of sequence produced a font in a sidecar file
beside it, which makes the distinction a property of the data and keeps it out of the analyst’s
memory.
   Transformation order can matter for similar reasons. Quantizing a curve before deforming
it need not produce the same outline as deforming it before quantization, because the second
operation acts on a different intermediate state. The repository advertises paired order-effect
experiments, including a wave-then-grid against grid-then-wave comparison at fixed intensity,
and contains viewers for comparing such paths. This is a productive extension of the font work
into questions of persistence and reconstruction.  It does not require claiming that a glyph
literally remembers. The final geometry can preserve consequences of the sequence through
which it was produced, and history becomes observable through differences between resulting
forms.
   The repository also treats the schedule of intensity along a document as a separate variable.
A small module of curve functions maps a position in the document to a distortion intensity,
with linear, quadratic, cubic, smoothstep, and cliff shapes. A cliff schedule stays near clean
until a chosen position and then ramps rapidly, and a quadratic schedule delays most of the
damage to the end. The same endpoint fonts under different schedules give a reader different
experiences of the same text, which is one more way in which the nominal intensity at a point
underdetermines what is encountered.
   The measurement code makes a useful epistemic distinction. It records representation-level
quantities such as numbers of points and contours, bounds, and a contour-length measure.
Such measurements characterize the stored geometry. They cannot, without reader evidence,
establish how legible a word is or whether its meaning remains recoverable. Small geometric
changes can remove a diagnostic dot, while large movements elsewhere can leave recognition
relatively undisturbed. A useful investigation therefore relates geometric state to performance
on a specified task instead of substituting one for the other. The repository documentation
explicitly acknowledges this limit.
    Its OCR experiments introduce another task with another kind of observer. The inspected
core renders words against a plain high-contrast background, submits the image to Tesseract,
and compares the output with the expected string.  This arrangement helps separate font-
related changes from additional background noise. However, an English OCR system failing
on Galactic substitutions is not by itself evidence that the text has become unreadable to a
practiced Galactic reader. Nor does such failure establish security against other recognition
systems.  It establishes a result for a particular recognition setup. Human reading, generic
OCR, and an OCR model trained on the relevant script can have substantially different success
conditions.

                                        10

Even the scoring method deserves specificity. The core uses Python’s SequenceMatcher to
derive an edit-like score by summing the larger side of each non-matching alignment block.
Each block can be realized by substituting the shared length and inserting or deleting the
remainder, so these operations define a valid edit sequence.  Its cost is therefore an upper
bound on the minimum Levenshtein distance, although it need not equal that minimum. With
the same normalization and clipping, the resulting character-accuracy score cannot exceed the
corresponding score calculated from the true minimum distance.  This bound follows from
the construction rather than from random sampling. It identifies what the reported quantity
measures, and the same care that distinguishes character mappings from glyph counts should
distinguish alignment-derived similarity from minimum edit distance.

8  Reader-side experiments

The principal opportunity opened by this collection is to study the relation between learned
recognition and changing inscription. The practices described above supply an unusual combi-
nation: a script that one reader has used daily as a working interface, and a generator that can
vary the inscription while holding the underlying character sequence fixed. The experiments
sketched here are proposals. None has been run, and none of the observations in the preceding
sections is evidence for how they would turn out.
   The first design varies the history of exposure while holding its amount constant. Initially
unfamiliar readers are randomly assigned to schedules containing the same material and the
same total exposure, with order, spacing, or progression manipulated between groups.  All
groups are then assessed on a common test containing held-out items. Both groups accumulate
experience: shuffling or resetting the displayed stimuli does not reset a reader’s learned state.
Differences on the common test would provide evidence that the manipulated exposure history
matters beyond its total amount, subject to controls for baseline ability and other differences
between groups.
   The second design varies the stimulus along a path while comparing readers with different
levels of familiarity. Practiced and initially unfamiliar readers encounter matched text through
a clean source face, an independent sweep, and a cumulative sequence ending at the same
nominal intensity, with text assignment and presentation order counterbalanced. A related
design compares wave-then-grid with grid-then-wave at matched parameter settings. A reliable
difference in recognition accuracy or response time would support a perceptual consequence
of transformation order under those conditions. Failure to detect a difference would leave the
geometric distinction intact and could reflect task insensitivity, limited statistical power, or a
difference without practical relevance to the tested task.
   The third design asks how well the geometric measurements predict recognition. The sidecar
measurements, the OCR scores, and reader accuracy and response time can be collected on the
same set of rendered words and compared. The repository’s own caution that its measurements
are geometric and do not establish legibility sets up the question, and the practiced and naive
readers serve as two different observers alongside generic OCR. A script-trained OCR model
would add a fourth.  Cheiro and Clypto, which preserve recognizable Latin reading while


                                        11

changing the drawn vocabulary, act as a control for effects of handwriting-like texture apart
from substitution.
   The fourth design uses the curve schedules. Because the position-to-intensity mapping is a
separate function, a document can be rendered under a linear schedule and under a cliff schedule
with identical endpoints. Recovery after added context, isolated letters against continuous text,
and the point at which a reader stops following the narrative are all measurable against position,
and the curve shape is the manipulated variable.
   These designs share several constraints that should be stated at the outset. Display size,
spacing, and fallback glyph substitution can change results, and a rendering pipeline should
fix them. A single practiced reader is a case study and cannot support a population claim,
so the practiced condition would need more than one reader. The recognition scores should
be reported with their method, for the reasons given in the preceding section.  Finally, the
sources of the transformed faces should be recorded as carefully as the transformations, since
an experimental result about a face of unrecorded provenance inherits that gap.

9  Preservation and conclusion

The collection invites a more precise account of preservation. Preserving a font file can preserve
outlines without preserving knowledge of its expected input. Preserving a private-use character
sequence can preserve code points without preserving the convention that gives them meaning.
Preserving a screenshot can preserve appearance while discarding the underlying character
identities. The repository’s mixture of fonts, source projects, scripts, text, and explanatory
material can help preserve several of these relations together. A future account of the manually
constructed faces would add another layer by recording which characters were drawn, borrowed,
transformed, or reassigned and why.
   The scale of SGA Regular becomes intelligible in this setting.  Its 14,208 entries record
much more than the visible alphabet on an introductory chart. They include practical accom-
modations, other scripts, registry-aligned material, diagnostic placeholders, and the residues
of a layered production history.  Cursive Galactic selects a smaller repertoire while giving
its everyday reading forms a different movement. Cheiro and Clypto investigate handwritten
Latin texture, Logico_philosophicus shifts prose toward the appearance of symbolic notation,
Lingojam_cipher depends on converted Unicode input, and the procedural experiments turn
established outlines into sequences of possible states. Their differences are part of the collec-
tion’s substance.
  What joins these activities is the work of making marks available for continued interpreta-
tion, and the distinction announced at the start returns here at every joint. A Sharpie stroke
becomes a vector outline, an outline acquires a character address, and a character becomes
part of an interface or subtitle, where repeated encounters let a reader proceed through it with
increasing familiarity. Each step is an operation on the previous state, and none of them is
fixed by a single intensity parameter. The same holds for the transformed faces, whose states
depend on whether they were generated from the source or from one another, and on the order
in which the operations were applied. The fonts are consequently valuable both as artifacts

of manual making and as instruments for studying how a reading environment, and a reader’s
place in it, come to be established. The strongest evidence available now is an ordinary act, a
viewer following a film in letters that were once drawn with a marker, and the proposals above
are an account of how to turn that act into a measurement.

Sources and method

The font counts, mappings, metadata, table inventories, spacing observations, and outline com-
parisons were obtained directly from downloaded files using FontTools.  Visual observations
refer to specimens rendered with Pillow, and no claim of exhaustive multilingual shaping or
perceptual validation is made. SGA Regular and Cursive Galactic in the fonts repository were
byte-for-byte identical to the copies previously examined in the alphabet repository. The units-
per-em value, the advance-width counts, and the table list of SGA Regular were rechecked
against the file at the examined commit. The discussion of the scoring bound follows an-
alytically from the edit sequence represented by the opcode calculation; no random-string
experiment is claimed. Private-use block occupancy was checked against registry allocations,
with selected outlines inspected rather than every assigned character certified. The counts of
repository files came from an untruncated recursive Git tree. Font metadata dates are retained
date strings rather than verified completion dates. Statements about Sharpie drawing, manual
work, system-font use, and VLC subtitles come from Flyxion’s account in the accompany-
ing conversation. The essay offers interpretation of those practices without presenting that
interpretation as experimental psychology.
